## The page removes some doubt, not all of it

A printed score trades some of the uncertainty of listening for visible claims
about pitch and duration. What it doesn't remove is interpretation. So keep the
two apart: preserve what the page says in one layer, and let a renderer decide
how Sonic Pi performs it in another.

Measure and beat references give that event list a coordinate system, and you'll
want one. "The third E sounds wrong" is almost impossible to investigate.
"Measure 2, beat 3 differs from the source" points straight at a comparison you
can make in ten seconds. Keep your [Lesson 42](42-finding-music-you-can-legally-use.qmd) source record nearby, because a
coordinate belongs to a particular edition. A pickup, an editorial division or a
variant measure can renumber everything after it.

Work one voice and one bar at a time. Fix the time and key signatures, then
handle rhythm, pitch, ties and articulation in that order. When a printed note
sounds strange next to a recording you know, write the disagreement down instead
of quietly bending the score to match what you expected. Page and performance
are two witnesses, and your transcription should say which one it followed.

## One event list, two renderings

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 72
use_synth :piano

events = [
  {measure: 1, note: :c4, start: 0.0, duration: 1.0},
  {measure: 1, note: :e4, start: 1.0, duration: 1.0},
  {measure: 1, note: :g4, start: 2.0, duration: 2.0},
  {measure: 2, note: :f4, start: 4.0, duration: 1.0},
  {measure: 2, note: :e4, start: 5.0, duration: 1.0},
  {measure: 2, note: :d4, start: 6.0, duration: 1.0},
  {measure: 2, note: :c4, start: 7.0, duration: 1.0}
]

define :play_events do |score, shaped|
  cursor = 0.0
  score.each_with_index do |event, index|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    phrase_amp = shaped ? 0.65 + (index * 0.05) : 0.8
    release = shaped ? event[:duration] * 0.82 : event[:duration]
    play event[:note], release: release, amp: phrase_amp
    cursor = event[:start]
  end
  sleep score.last[:duration]
end

play_events events, false
sleep 1
play_events events, true
```

Both passes attack the same pitches at the same moments. In the second, each
note is a shade louder than the last and its release is shorter, which gives you
a gentle growth and slightly narrower gaps. Every one of those audible changes
belongs to the renderer. The event list stays a checkable claim about what's
printed on the page.

The measure numbers ride along and never reach Sonic Pi. Why carry a field the
renderer ignores? Because in three months it's the only thing standing between a
doubtful note and a re-transcription.

## Break the score, then break the interpretation

1. Shorten the G in measure 1 from 2.0 to 1.5. Measure 2 still starts at global
   4.0, so a half-beat hole opens before F. That silence identifies a damaged
   duration without shifting a single later event.
2. Restore the G, then change the shaped amplitude to subtract `index * 0.04`.
   Only the interpreted rendering recedes. Check the array afterwards: no pitch,
   start, duration, measure or source claim should have moved.
3. Add a `source_page` field, either on every event or on a score object wrapped
   around the array, and print measure and page before each attack. Playback is
   identical. A disputed note is now much faster to find on the original.

## Why the score layer is immutable

Treat it as input. The renderer transforms that input into timed Sonic Pi calls
and never rewrites the evidence it was handed. One transcription can then feed
several interpretations, and your duration and alignment checks can run before
reverb, envelopes and performance dynamics muddy what you're hearing.

Ties are where notation and sounding events stop being one-to-one. A tie joins
durations of the same pitch into one sustained sound, not a second attack.
Encode the sounding event, and keep a comment or a field describing the tie for
anyone who later needs the printed detail. A slur or phrase mark usually changes
articulation without changing event count, so that belongs in a field the
renderer reads.

Accidentals need the scoped resolver from [Lesson 40](../08-reading-notation/40-key-signatures-defaults.qmd). Start from the key
signature default, apply any accidental governing that pitch within the bar,
then convert the resolved spelling to a note or MIDI number, and reset the
bar-local map at the bar line. A measure-by-measure representation makes that
scope visible, which is what stops an F-sharp leaking into the next measure
because a mutable map never got cleared.

When score and recording disagree, keep both observations, separately. The
performer might have altered the rhythm, the edition might differ, or the
recording might use an ornament the page never mentions. You're not trying to
force the witnesses into agreement. You're keeping the source-faithful layer
precise enough that an interpretive renderer can depart from it on purpose.

## Encode eight measures, then interpret them twice

Pick a short public-domain score from the inventory you built in [Lesson 42](42-finding-music-you-can-legally-use.qmd).
Encode at least eight measures of one voice with exact pitch, global start and
duration. Attach source page and measure references, and annotate ties or
unclear print wherever they affected a decision you made.

Then produce a score-strict rendering and a performance-shaped one from the same
array. Prove the separation: change articulation, dynamics or synth in the
renderer, run both again, and confirm the transcribed data is byte-identical. If
you had to touch the events to get the interpretation you wanted, the boundary
leaked, and finding where is the real work of this exercise.
